Indigenous mother tongues in the Canadian census

What can census tables tell us about Indigenous mother tongues across provinces?

Project walkthrough

DATA 201 · Group project
Exploring Canadian census language patterns using provincial tables.

Rreadxlggplot2Census data
My contribution

I proposed the project topic, completed analysis question three on Indigenous mother tongues, and contributed to the report and presentation introduction.

Process & technical work

Imported provincial Excel sheets into R with readxl, extracted Indigenous mother-tongue counts and “Neither English nor French” counts, converted values to numeric, and visualized provincial comparisons with ggplot2.

Outcome & what I learned

Developed an R workflow for comparing provincial population counts and derived percentages. This project also offers a valuable opportunity to revisit whether a metric answers the intended question.

Limitations & next steps

The report uses first-official-language categories as a retention proxy. This does not directly measure continued use of a mother tongue at home. I would validate the variable definitions and rebuild a retention metric before presenting those percentages as retention rates.

What to look for

I proposed the topic and owned analysis question three. The chart uses first official language spoken as a proxy. A direct measure would compare mother tongue with language spoken at home.

SECTION A: INTRODUCTION (2%)



Language plays a central role in shaping cultural identity, community belonging, and social

integration. In multilingual countries such as Canada - where over 200 languages are spoken -

understanding whether individuals maintain their mother tongue across generations provides

valuable insight into cultural continuity and demographic change. This project investigates

patterns of language retention in Canada, focusing on the extent to which individuals

continue to speak their mother tongue at home and how this varies across provinces, age

groups, and language communities. Our main objective is to measure and visualize mother

tongue retention using reliable national data, then interpret the patterns within Canada’s

unique linguistic landscape.


Language retention is especially important in Canada because of its official bilingualism

policies, long  history  of immigration, and strong Indigenous and immigrant language

communities. The 2021 Census shows that millions of Canadians report a mother tongue

other than English and French, yet not all continue to use that language most often at home.

Retention rates can reflect cultural attachment, generational shifts, government language

policies, and the influence of dominant languages within specific regions. For example,

Quebec’s French-language protections may encourage different retention outcomes compared

to provinces where English  is  the overwhelming majority language. Similarly, newer

immigrant groups may have higher retention due to strong community networks, while

third-generation speakers often shift toward English or French. These dynamics make Canada

an ideal case study for analyzing how languages survive - or fade - over time.


To explore these issues, we use Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0169-01 from the 2021 Census,

a comprehensive dataset that reports mother tongues, first official language spoken, and

languages spoken at home across all provinces and territories. Using this dataset allows us to

calculate  retention  rates,  compare  patterns  across  regions, and  identify  generational

differences with precision and consistency. By analyzing this publicly available census data,

we aim to uncover meaningful trends in how Canadians maintain their linguistic heritage and

what social, cultural, or regional factors may be influencing these outcomes.

    2.​ Which territories or provinces show the lowest and highest retention rates

      of mother tongue, and what factors might contribute to these differences?



      Across Canada, the retention of an individual’s mother tongue highlights a compelling

linguistic map of cultural persistence and adaptation. Using Statistics Canada dataset on

“Mother Tongue by First Official Language Spoken” we can identify which provinces and

territories demonstrate the lowest and highest rates of language retention and explore the

factors that sustain or erase an individual’s mother tongue across the country. Provinces like

Quebec, and New Brunswick have the strongest mother tongue retention rates. Quebec is one

of the leading mother tongue retention for the French Canadian language with 6,909,565 out

of 8,406,905. In Quebec, French is not just a language but an important part in their collective

identity, supported by decades of education, policies and media. Second is New Brunswick

with 528,555 speaking English as their native tongue out of 764,630. Only 1,710 speak

neither English or French which  is one of the lowest in Canada. In New Brunswick,

bilingualism thrives under constitutional protection, giving both French and English speakers

a sense of consistency in their linguistic traditions. In contrast, British Columbia, Ontario,

and Alberta have the lowest retention rates of mother tongues, particularly among speakers of

non official languages. Alberta has roughly a 1.51%, Ontario is 2.39%, and British Columbia

has a 3.21% for mother tongue retention for non official speaking languages. In these

provinces, English is the leading mother tongue. In Alberta English being the mother tongue

is 96.6% out of 4,221,835, Ontario is 93.47% out of 14,099,790 and British Columbia is

Page 13

95.29% out of 4,951,655. It’s used everyday and everywhere in education, employment, and

public life which leads to immigrant families eventually shifting more towards the use of

English. The social pressure to conform to an English speaking environment combined with

the limited minority communities, accelerates the erosion of these separate languages.

    3.​ How do Indigenous mother tongues compare to other languages in terms

      of retention rates across Canada?



 ​     To explore this question, I first brought the provincial census tables into R from the

Excel file using the “readxl” package. Each province had its own sheet, so I read them one by

one and pulled out the rows and columns that contained Indigenous mother-tongue counts.

For  every  province,  I  recorded two key numbers:  the  total number  of  Indigenous

mother-tongue speakers, and the number of Indigenous speakers who fell into the “Neither

English nor French” category. These values were stored into a single data frame and

converted to numeric format so that retention rate percentages could be calculated for each

province. Finally, using ggplot2, I created bar charts showing Indigenous speaker counts and

retention rates by province; these graphs form the basis of the discussion that follows.




​      Bar  charts  were  chosen  because  they  make  provincial  comparisons  very

straightforward for the reader. Each province appears as its own bar, so it is easy to see where

Indigenous populations are larger or smaller. The first chart focuses on the size of Indigenous

mother-tongue population in each province, helping to set context for the rest of the analysis.

The second chart uses the same provinces and ordering but displays retention percentage

instead, allowing us to immediately compare population size with the strength of language

retention. Keeping the same visual style for both charts creates a consistent story: first we see

how many Indigenous speakers are there, and then we see how many of them are likely to be

maintaining Indigenous or non-official languages instead of shifting toward English or

French.

Page 15

Data Visualizations:





Figure E.4​      ​           ​           ​           ​           Figure E.5




      Looking across the provinces, the visualizations reveal a very uneven picture of

Indigenous language retention in Canada. Some regions show relatively strong continuity of

Indigenous mother tongues, while others exhibit clear signs of language shift toward English

or French. In Quebec, for example, there are about 41,820 Indigenous mother-tongue

speakers, and roughly 2,685 of them fall into the “Neither English nor French” category,

yielding the highest retention rate at approximately 6.4%. Newfoundland and Labrador has a

much smaller Indigenous-speaking population of about 1,835 people, yet around 60 of them

are in this category, which corresponds to a retention rate of roughly 3.3%. By contrast,

several provinces show very low retention: Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, and

Manitoba all have between about 0.5% and 0.9% retention, despite Indigenous totals ranging

from 5,490  to 20,785  speakers. New Brunswick has 1,715 Indigenous mother-tongue

speakers but only about five in “Neither English nor French” category, giving a retention rate

of just 0.3%, and Prince Edward Island has 45 Indigenous speakers with no recorded cases in

this category, indicating no measurable retention under our definition.



     When these patterns are considered alongside the results for English, French and

non-official languages presented in Question 2, Indigenous mother tongues generally appear

Page 16

to face greater challenges in being maintained over time. Official languages tend to have high

and stable retention within their dominant regions, and some immigrant language groups also

maintain  relatively  strong  retention  in  provinces  with  large  and  well-established

communities. In many areas, however, Indigenous languages seem more vulnerable to shift,

likely  reflecting  a  combination  of  historical  disruption,  smaller  or more  dispersed

communities, and institutional pressure to use English or French in education and public life.

Taken together, the Indigenous-focused findings suggest that, compared with other language

groups in Canada, Indigenous mother tongues require stronger support and favourable local

conditions to be preserved across generations.





    4.​ What does mother tongue retention look like for multilingual individuals

      across the Canadian provinces?



       Multilingualism differs quite a bit across the Canadian provinces, which makes sense

as there is much variability in culture across Canada. Each province has its own distinct

culture, for example Quebec is predominantly Francophone, and provinces such as Ontario

and British Columbia that are giant melting pots of diversity and culture.




      According to the dataset,  it appears that in almost every province the multilingual

people who were able to retain their mother tongue are those whose first language is neither

French nor English. A logical explanation for this could be the absence of non-official

languages within the vast majority of public society,  and more specifically, within the

education systems. Recognizing this, it is easy to assume that families intentionally use their

mother tongue languages at home, knowing the official Canadian languages – English and

French – will be taught and learned naturally in school and society. The only provinces that

do not fit into this blanket statement are Quebec and New Brunswick. This makes sense as

these provinces have the two highest percentages of French speakers in Canada.

Page 17

      Quebec has the greatest total retention of multilingual official language speakers at

almost 330,000 people. To compare the other end of the spectrum, Newfoundland and

Labrador has the lowest total retention of multilingual official language speakers at only 300

people. Quebec has a very large data range because it has a high population, and a significant

amount of that population is individuals who speak both French and English. Newfoundland

and Labrador in comparison, has a very small data range because of its low population, where

most are Native English speakers.




       Ontario has the greatest total retention of multilingual non-official language speakers

with almost 340,000 people. British Columbia also has quite a high number with about

159,000 people, especially in comparison to its 18,000 official language multilinguals. This

makes sense as both Ontario and British Columbia have regions with very high population

density especially compared to the rest of the province. Ontario has the Greater Toronto Area

with a population of about 6.2 million people, and British Columbia has the Lower Mainland

with a population of just over 3 million. In addition, these provinces also have the top two

greatest immigration rates within Canada.




       Overall, it is evident that there is a large variance of mother tongue language retention

for  multilingual Canadians across  the  provinces. This makes sense as there  is much

variability in culture across Canada, with Quebec being predominantly Francophone, and

provinces such as Ontario and British Columbia that are giant melting pots of diversity and

culture. Looking at the graphs  it is obvious that the multilingual people who retain their

mother tongue best, are those whose first language is not an official Canadian language.

    5.​ How does mother tongue  retention  differ among Canada’s  official

      language groups (English and French) and non-official language groups?



Data Visualizations :





 Figure E.8​     ​           ​           ​           ​           ​      Figure E.9




      The  horizontal  bar  graph  visualization  provides  a  generic  comparison  of

mother-tongue retention across three scales, namely Alberta, Québec, and the national

average. This allows us to compare both regional patterns and see how each province aligns

with nationwide trends.




For English, retention is extremely high nationwide. Alberta’s retention rate is 99.9959%,

which is essentially perfect, rounding up to 100% in the slope diagram visualization. Québec

sits slightly lower at 99.22%, likely reflecting the influence of French as the dominant

language in the province. The bar graph also shows these values to be near equal to the

national average, reinforcing that English is consistently maintained across generations in

nearly every province. Another factor contributing to these high retention rates may include

the second generation immigrants, who report English as their first language for official

purposes, even though they continue speaking a heritage language at home with parents or

grandparents.

Page 20

      For French, the bar graph reveals much stronger regional contrast. Québec shows an

exceptionally high but expected retention rate of 99.96%, reflecting its large francophone

population. Alberta’s French retention rate is notably lower at 90.64%, while Saskatchewan

(shown in the dataset but not the slope graph) is even lower at 84.32%, illustrating how

French speakers represent a minority status in the province.




       Non-official languages show a completely different pattern. Retention is extremely

low across Canada compared to the official languages. Alberta’s retention rate sits at 6.97%

and Québec’s at 6.72%, demonstrating a significant language and potentially even cultural

shift. British Columbia (in the dataset) reaches the highest non-official retention, 11.43%,

likely reflecting its growing immigrant communities. Both the bar graph and slope graph

visualizations, each highlight the vast contrast between official and non-official languages

immediately visible.




      The slope graph provides a more focused, province based comparison of Alberta and

Québec. For English, the slope graph shows an almost perfectly horizontal  line, with

Alberta’s retention rounds to 100% (from 99.9959%) and Québec slightly downwards at

99.22%, making the difference appear minimal. For French, the slope graph shows a steep

downward slope from Québec (99.96%) to Alberta (90.64%), visually emphasizing the

noticeable regional gap in French retention. The most interesting comparison is highlighted

by the line for non-official languages, both of which stay low and nearly flat with Alberta

(6.97%) and Québec (6.72%), showing that both provinces experience very similar low levels

of heritage language retention.
